facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Leverage was moderate before 2025 and is high on any basis that can be measured. At the end of 2024 total debt was 3.22x and net debt 3.09x reported EBITDA. Reported EBITDA then turned negative because the company took non-cash impairment charges of USD 1.01 billion in 2025, almost all of it goodwill, so the 2025 and last-twelve-month ratios on the reported basis are not calculable. Excluding impairment, legal settlements, debt extinguishment and property sale results, net debt was 3.01x EBITDA at the end of 2024, 5.72x at the end of 2025 and 4.96x at 2026-09-30, with gross debt at 5.33x. Basis: calculation C9; calculation C10; calculation N1; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 88; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 122

rows.label: Chart data: revenue and EBITDA — paragraph 1

limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- No filing states EBITDA, so reported EBITDA is derived and the credit agreement's Consolidated EBITDA is not available; this restricts every leverage and cover ratio and the reported ratios for 2025 and the last twelve months are not calculable because derived EBITDA is negative (High). Supply the compliance certificate or an earnings release with the covenant reconciliation. - Covenant ratios and covenant earnings are not printed, only the levels and a statement of compliance, so headroom cannot be calculated (High). Supply the compliance certificate. - Cash paid for interest and for income taxes is not printed in the 2026 quarterly reports, so cash interest cover for the last twelve months and cash taxes for 2026 are not calculable (Medium). Supply the nine-month cash flow supplement. - The margin in force on the term loan and revolver is not stated (the grid runs from 1.375% to 2.250% over the reference rate) and no floor is stated, so cash interest cannot be reconciled to debt (Medium). Supply the pricing certificate or the credit agreement. - Carrying value by instrument is not disclosed, only one aggregate of unamortized issuance costs, discount and premium, so the debt table carries principal by instrument and one financing cost adjustment (Low). - Maintenance and growth capital expenditure are not split in the filings, so only total capital expenditure is carried, and the 2026 fall in spending cannot be classified as discretionary or maintenance (Medium). Supply management's capital plan. - No fourth quarter of 2025 is reported, so it is derived as the year less nine months; quarterly balance sheets before 2026 and net debt at 2023-12-31 are not tabulated (Low). - The statement of income is by nature of expense, so cost of sales, gross profit and a selling and administrative subtotal are not supplied (Low). No action. - Lines printed as a dash, or absent from a period's statement, are carried as not supplied and never as zero, including the provider relief fund line, debt extinguishment costs and the noncontrolling distributions line in the first quarter of 2026 (Low). - The 2025 year-end guarantor summarised figures exist in two versions, the annual report's and the revised version in the 2026 quarterly reports, which the company calls an immaterial correction; both are kept as printed and the later governs (Low). - The relative rank of the three series of senior notes is not stated in so many words; they are shown at one rank because each is described as senior and guaranteed on the same basis (Low). - Per-share data and weighted-average shares are not tabulated, and the filings identify no restricted cash (Low). - Facility and bed counts at September 2025 and at 2023, and same-facility rates for the first nine months of 2025 and for 2023, are not in the filings, so the operating dashboard has gaps in those periods (Low). - The October 2026 payment to plaintiffs' counsel is dated to the month only, so no day is stated for the post-balance-sheet adjustment (Low).

facts.text: The strongest evidence against a Medium rating is that no behaviour in the filings extracts value from creditors: no dividend, a paused repurchase, cut capital spending, USD 147.61 million less debt than at the end of 2025 and no state above 14% of revenue or facility above 4%. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a weak view is the direction of travel: house-normalised net leverage fell from 5.72x to 4.96x, free cash flow turned positive at USD 155.62 million in the nine months, debt fell USD 147.61 million and no behaviour in the filings extracts value from creditors. The strongest evidence for a weaker view is that the improvement comes mainly from cutting capital spending, the earnings base used for leverage is a house measure, and legal outcomes are unquantified. The view would improve if the investigations close without a material penalty, same-facility growth holds while capital spending stays low for a further year, and the compliance certificate shows covenant room on the agreement's own definition. It would worsen if Medicaid directed-payment caps or eligibility rules reduce revenue per patient day, if an investigation or the contested jury award produces a payment near the scale of the Desert Hills settlement, or if repurchases or growth spending resume before the 2028 notes are refinanced. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C5; calculation N11

facts.label: Company description
facts.text: Acadia runs 280 behavioral healthcare facilities with about 12,800 beds in 40 states and Puerto Rico through the subsidiaries of a listed holding company. Acute inpatient psychiatric care was 55% of 2025 revenue, specialty treatment 17%, comprehensive treatment centers for opioid use 17% and residential treatment 11%. Demand is clinical and non-discretionary and entry is limited by licensing and certificate-of-need rules, which supports volume visibility, but 72% of revenue comes from Medicare and Medicaid at predetermined rate schedules, so cash-flow visibility rests on government budgets and the company cannot recover cost increases through price. facts.text: No sponsor or controlling holder is identified, so there is no extraction vehicle and no equity backstop; the only investor named, Waud Capital Partners, has a charter carve-out and no stated stake. facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Revenue is predictable in volume but not in price. Same-facility revenue grew 4.0% in the nine months of 2026, with patient days up 1.2%, admissions up 6.5% and revenue per patient day up 2.8%, so growth is admission and price led while stays shorten. Government payors reimburse on predetermined rate schedules and Medicaid supplied 61.8% of revenue against 53.9% in 2023, which ties pricing power to state budgets and to the federal budget act that caps state directed payments from 2028. Consolidated revenue grew 5.04% in 2025 and 3.96% in the nine months of 2026, and the shift of mix toward acute inpatient care increases dependence on the line under investigation. facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Margins have compressed and the cost base is largely fixed. Salaries, wages and benefits were 55.27% of nine-month 2026 revenue, the company reports a shortage of nurses and counselors that forces wage increases and costlier contract labor, and other operating expenses, mainly purchased services, insurance and provider taxes, rose to 16.7% of 2025 revenue from 14.0% and were 16.3% in the nine months of 2026 with a USD 28.6 million unfavourable liability adjustment. House-normalised EBITDA margin fell to 12.48% in 2025 from 19.82% in 2024 and was 12.94% for the last twelve months, so margins cannot be defended under volume pressure without cost action, and cost flexibility sits mainly in growth capital spending rather than operating costs. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The initiating condition is a Medicaid rate or eligibility reduction, such as a state directed payment cap, arriving in the same period as an enforcement outcome. The first operational break is revenue per patient day, because government rate schedules do not rise with cost while salaries, wages and benefits are 55.27% of revenue, so margin falls faster than revenue. The financial transmission is lower house-normalised EBITDA against fixed debt, which lifts leverage above the 4.96x reached at 2026-09-30, while a settlement of the scale of the USD 400.0 million paid in 2024 would equal 45.80% of current liquidity of USD 873.41 million. The liquidity consequence is manageable through 2028 because liquidity covers scheduled principal 1.63 times, but the refinancing consequence is severe if leverage is high when the 2028 notes must be refinanced. Management levers are growth capital spending, held-for-sale property, the paused repurchase program and revolver availability; the observable triggers are same-facility revenue per patient day, the Medicaid share of revenue and any investigation development. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress through 2028 absent a combined shock. ## Request

Source readiness for Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc. (issuer achc-1520697), as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is whether the five supplied filings can support the selected analysis, and which gaps and conflicts limit it.

## Findings
### Bottom line
The five Acadia filings support a snapshot of reported financials, debt terms and liquidity through the quarter ended 2026-09-30, but they cannot test covenants, security or relative value.

No executed credit agreement or indenture, credit rating, market price, peer set or fund limit was supplied, and the filings print no covenant-basis earnings figure, so every statement about debt protections rests on the company's own summaries. One conflict is open: the company later revised its year-end 2025 guarantor figures, so two versions of them exist.

spans.text: # CP-1 Financial foundation: Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc. (achc-1520697)
## Request

Financial foundation for Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc. (issuer achc-1520697), as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is the consolidated statements, debt, liquidity and derived periods for the five supplied filings, latest period the quarter ended 2026-09-30.
## Sources

## Findings
### Bottom line

Reported EBITDA is negative for 2025 and the last twelve months, so reported leverage is not measurable; after excluding impairment and legal settlements, net leverage is 4.96x at 2026-09-30, a house-normalised figure that is not the covenant measure.
Basis: calculation C10; calculation C8; calculation C7; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 122; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 3

Net debt fell to USD 2.19 billion at 2026-09-30 from USD 2.37 billion at the end of 2025 as capital spending was cut and revolver borrowings were repaid, and USD 710.1 million of the revolver was undrawn. Cash interest cover was 5.36x in 2024 and is not calculable for the last twelve months because the quarterly reports print no cash interest.
Basis: calculation C4; calculation N2; calculation N3; calculation C16; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 22
### Key findings

Leverage was moderate before 2025 and is high on any basis that can be measured. At the end of 2024 total debt was 3.22x and net debt 3.09x reported EBITDA. Reported EBITDA then turned negative because the company took non-cash impairment charges of USD 1.01 billion in 2025, almost all of it goodwill, so the 2025 and last-twelve-month ratios on the reported basis are not calculable. Excluding impairment, legal settlements, debt extinguishment and property sale results, net debt was 3.01x EBITDA at the end of 2024, 5.72x at the end of 2025 and 4.96x at 2026-09-30, with gross debt at 5.33x.
Basis: calculation C9; calculation C10; calculation N1; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 88; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 122

The step-up in 2025 came from gross debt rising by USD 543.06 million while capital spending of USD 571.81 million far exceeded operating cash flow. Debt has since fallen by USD 147.61 million to USD 2.35 billion at 2026-09-30, and house-normalised EBITDA rose from USD 413.58 million for 2025 to USD 441.51 million for the last twelve months; both moves, in roughly equal measure, took the house-normalised net ratio from 5.72x to 4.96x.

Basis: calculation N5; calculation N6; calculation N4; calculation N12; calculation N20; calculation N21; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 123; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 4

Free cash flow was an outflow of USD 560.69 million in 2024, when the January 2024 payment of USD 400.0 million under the Desert Hills settlement agreements fell within a USD 420.89 million cash outflow in accounts payable and other accrued liabilities, and an outflow of USD 439.91 million in 2025. In the first nine months of 2026 free cash flow was positive at USD 155.62 million, against an outflow of USD 260.43 million a year earlier, because cash paid for capital expenditures fell to USD 165.86 million from USD 478.62 million while operating cash flow rose to USD 321.48 million from USD 218.19 million. Over the last twelve months free cash flow is still slightly negative, so the improvement depends on capital spending staying low.

Basis: calculation C12; calculation N8; calculation N18; calculation N7; calculation N9; calculation N10; calculation N11; calculation N13; calculation N14; 10-K_2024-12-31_achc_achc-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 125; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 123; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5

Cash paid for interest was USD 124.66 million in 2025 against interest expense, net of USD 138.86 million. Reported EBITDA covered cash interest 5.36x in 2024 and was negative 5.92x in 2025; on the house-normalised basis cover was 5.51x in 2024 and 3.32x in 2025, so cover weakened sharply as debt rose and earnings fell.
Basis: calculation C11; calculation N15; calculation N16; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 122–123

Liquidity at 2026-09-30 was USD 873.41 million of cash plus the undrawn revolver, after standby letters of credit rose to USD 15.9 million from USD 1.2 million three months earlier. Term-loan repayments are modest, but the revolver and the term-loan balance fall due together in 2030 (USD 745.05 million of principal), with the 2028 notes and term-loan repayments (USD 494.73 million) and the 2029 notes (USD 536.10 million) ahead of them and the 2033 notes of USD 550.00 million last.

Basis: calculation C16; calculation N17; calculation C13; calculation N22; calculation N23; calculation N24; calculation N25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 20–23; 10-Q_2026-06-30_achc_achc-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 22

Revenue grew 5.04% in 2025 and 3.96% in the first nine months of 2026, but same-facility revenue growth slowed to 4.0% in the nine months from 7.7% in 2024, and the payor mix shifted toward Medicaid, which reached 61.8% of revenue from 56.5% in 2024 as the commercial share fell to 21.4% from 26.0%. A larger government-payor share exposes earnings to state Medicaid funding and rate decisions.

Basis: calculation C17; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 85; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 134; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 38

No filing states EBITDA, so every EBITDA figure here is derived from the statements and the credit agreement's own measure is unavailable. The house-normalised figure adds back a net USD 1,151.41 million in 2025, an Analyst Judgement that moves 2025 EBITDA from negative to USD 413.58 million. Debt at carrying value is USD 14.14 million below principal of USD 2,366.50 million; leases sit outside debt, and redeemable noncontrolling interests of USD 229.88 million sit outside both debt and equity.

Basis: calculation C6; calculation C8; calculation N19; calculation N20; calculation C14; calculation N26; calculation N27; calculation N28; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 20
### Limitations
- Cash paid for interest and for income taxes is printed only in the annual reports, so interest cover for the last twelve months and cash taxes for 2026 are not calculable.
- Covenant earnings and ratios are not printed, so the house-normalised ratios are not covenant measures and no headroom is stated.
- The quarterly balance sheets before 2026 and the fourth quarter of 2025 are not in the filings, so quarterly leverage before 2026 is not calculated and the fourth quarter is derived.
- Per-share data and weighted-average shares are not tabulated.

## Gaps

- No filing states EBITDA, so reported EBITDA is derived and the credit agreement's Consolidated EBITDA is not available; this restricts every leverage and cover ratio and the reported ratios for 2025 and the last twelve months are not calculable because derived EBITDA is negative (High). Supply the compliance certificate or an earnings release with the covenant reconciliation.
- Covenant ratios and covenant earnings are not printed, only the levels and a statement of compliance, so headroom cannot be calculated (High). Supply the compliance certificate.

- Cash paid for interest and for income taxes is not printed in the 2026 quarterly reports, so cash interest cover for the last twelve months and cash taxes for 2026 are not calculable (Medium). Supply the nine-month cash flow supplement.

- The margin in force on the term loan and revolver is not stated (the grid runs from 1.375% to 2.250% over the reference rate) and no floor is stated, so cash interest cannot be reconciled to debt (Medium). Supply the pricing certificate or the credit agreement.

- Carrying value by instrument is not disclosed, only one aggregate of unamortized issuance costs, discount and premium, so the debt table carries principal by instrument and one financing cost adjustment (Low).

- Maintenance and growth capital expenditure are not split in the filings, so only total capital expenditure is carried, and the 2026 fall in spending cannot be classified as discretionary or maintenance (Medium). Supply management's capital plan.
- No fourth quarter of 2025 is reported, so it is derived as the year less nine months; quarterly balance sheets before 2026 and net debt at 2023-12-31 are not tabulated (Low).
- The statement of income is by nature of expense, so cost of sales, gross profit and a selling and administrative subtotal are not supplied (Low). No action.

- Lines printed as a dash, or absent from a period's statement, are carried as not supplied and never as zero, including the provider relief fund line, debt extinguishment costs and the noncontrolling distributions line in the first quarter of 2026 (Low).

- The 2025 year-end guarantor summarised figures exist in two versions, the annual report's and the revised version in the 2026 quarterly reports, which the company calls an immaterial correction; both are kept as printed and the later governs (Low).
- The relative rank of the three series of senior notes is not stated in so many words; they are shown at one rank because each is described as senior and guaranteed on the same basis (Low).
- Per-share data and weighted-average shares are not tabulated, and the filings identify no restricted cash (Low).

- Facility and bed counts at September 2025 and at 2023, and same-facility rates for the first nine months of 2025 and for 2023, are not in the filings, so the operating dashboard has gaps in those periods (Low).
- The October 2026 payment to plaintiffs' counsel is dated to the month only, so no day is stated for the post-balance-sheet adjustment (Low).

spans.text: # CP-1A Business & governance: Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc. (achc-1520697)
## Request

Business, ownership and governance facts for Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc. (issuer achc-1520697), as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is the company's business, structure, ownership, operating model, capital allocation and governance behaviour as stated in the five supplied filings.
## Sources

## Findings
### Bottom line

Acadia has no sponsor in the filings, so creditor risk comes from payor concentration and legal exposure, not owner extraction: Medicaid supplied 61.8% of revenue in nine months 2026 and a federal criminal investigation of the acute care line is open.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 74

No dividend has ever been paid and share repurchases stopped at USD 50.4 million in 2025, but 2025 capital spending was debt-funded and the chief executive and chief financial officer changed in 2026. Governance risk is assessed as Medium because the evidence is mixed and the proxy statement with board and holder detail was not supplied.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 78; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 79; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 54; 10-Q_2026-03-31_achc_achc-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 47; 10-Q_2026-06-30_achc_achc-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 54; calculation N1; calculation N3
### Key findings

The filings identify no controlling holder or sponsor, so creditors face no owner-extraction mechanism but also no sponsor equity to cure a shortfall. The company is a NASDAQ-listed holding company, the only investor named is Waud Capital Partners and it appears only in a charter clause that exempts it and its funds from the business-combination limit, with no stake stated, and the holder list sits in a proxy statement that was not supplied.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 74; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 108–110; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 1

Payor concentration is the dominant operating risk and it is rising. Medicaid was 57.7% of 2025 revenue and 61.8% of the first nine months of 2026, up from 53.9% in 2023, and Medicare and Medicaid together were about 72% of 2025 revenue. The federal 2025 budget act cuts Medicaid spending, bars new provider taxes and caps state directed payments, with grandfathered programs stepping down by ten percentage points a year from 2028; the company expects little near-term effect from the work requirements because of exemptions, but the payment caps would reduce the rate base behind its largest payor.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 42; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 134; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 36–37

Legal and regulatory exposure is the main event risk and it sits on the largest line. A federal grand jury investigation and SEC subpoenas concern the acute care line, which was 55% of 2025 revenue and 57.53% of nine-month 2026 revenue, covering admissions, length of stay and billing; the company reports no findings and cannot estimate a liability. Settled matters show the cash scale: USD 400.0 million for Desert Hills, USD 179.0 million for the 2019 securities class action with USD 31.5 million insured, and a 2026 jury award of USD 35.0 million compensatory and USD 70.0 million punitive damages against an indirect subsidiary that the subsidiary is contesting.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 20; calculation C3

Insurance does not absorb all of this, which turns verdicts into cash calls. Coverage for the relevant policy year was exhausted by prior losses for the sixth Desert Hills lawsuit and for the excess portion of the Sandoval settlement, and the self-insured professional and general liability reserve rose to USD 214.7 million from USD 181.8 million after a USD 28.6 million unfavourable adjustment in the second quarter of 2026.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 19

Leadership is in transition during the investigations. The chief executive agreement dated 2026-01-19 and the former chief executive's separation dated 2026-01-20 were followed by an interim chief financial officer who signs the second and third-quarter reports, and the returning chief executive holds a one-time option award that vests on share-price hurdles rather than credit measures. Finance continuity is therefore a monitoring point, not a finding of weakness.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-03-31_achc_achc-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 47; 10-Q_2026-03-31_achc_achc-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 48; 10-Q_2026-06-30_achc_achc-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 54; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 27

Capital allocation has not favoured shareholders at creditors' expense, but growth has been debt-funded. The company has never paid a dividend, used USD 50.4 million of a USD 300.0 million repurchase program in 2025 and none in 2026, leaving USD 250.0 million unused, while 2025 capital spending of USD 571.81 million far exceeded operating cash flow and total debt rose by USD 543.06 million; spending then fell to USD 165.86 million in the nine months of 2026.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 78; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 79; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 123; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 54; calculation N1; calculation N3

Growth is concentrated in acute inpatient care, which is also the line under investigation: acute revenue grew 8.05% in the nine months of 2026 while specialty treatment fell 7.72% and comprehensive treatment centers were flat, so the mix is moving toward the line with the largest regulatory overhang.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 9; calculation C3
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a Medium rating is that no behaviour in the filings extracts value from creditors: no dividend, a paused repurchase, cut capital spending, USD 147.61 million less debt than at the end of 2025 and no state above 14% of revenue or facility above 4%. The strongest evidence for a higher rating is the open criminal investigation, the rising Medicaid share and uninsured verdicts.

The view would move to Low if the investigations close without charges or a material penalty and Medicaid rate caps are absorbed without margin loss. It would move to High if the investigations produce charges, exclusion risk or a settlement near the scale of the Desert Hills payment, if the contested 2026 jury award is upheld without relief, or if buybacks or debt-funded growth resume while leverage is above its recent range.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 79; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 20; calculation N4
### Limitations

- The proxy statement was not supplied, so board composition, executive pay and holder concentration are not established; the ownership finding is limited to the absence of an identified controlling holder in the filings.
- Neither the credit agreement nor the indentures were supplied, so capacity for shareholder payments is not assessed and the no-extraction view rests on observed behaviour alone.

- The investigations and the contested jury award are unresolved with no liability range, so the legal figures here are settled amounts and not an estimate of future cost, which caps how far the Medium rating can be tightened.
- The finance leadership change is evidenced only by signature blocks and exhibit titles, so the date of the chief financial officer change is not established.
### Company and operating model
| Item | Detail | Source |

spans.text: # CP-2 Fundamental credit: Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc. (achc-1520697)
## Request

Fundamental credit analysis of Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc. (issuer achc-1520697), as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is the issuer's business, structure, earnings, cash flow, liquidity, refinancing and downside, synthesised from the five supplied filings and the three earlier analyses.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Acadia is a large, mostly owned behavioral healthcare operator whose credit is constrained by high leverage, near-zero free cash flow and open Medicaid and legal risks, so creditors depend on capital spending staying low and a clean investigation outcome.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A)

Net debt was USD 2.19 billion at 2026-09-30, 4.96x house-normalised EBITDA, because reported EBITDA is negative after a non-cash impairment; liquidity of USD 873.41 million exceeds the USD 535.35 million of principal due through 2028, but the 2028 to 2030 maturities will need refinancing.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C1; calculation N1; calculation N2
### Key findings

Leverage is the weakest dimension and the earnings base is clouded. Reported EBITDA is negative for 2025 and the last twelve months after USD 1.01 billion of non-cash impairment, so the usable measure is house-normalised: net debt was 3.01x EBITDA at the end of 2024, 5.72x at the end of 2025 and 4.96x at 2026-09-30. The covenant measure is not available, so no headroom is inferred, and the ratio is high enough that an earnings miss would reach refinancing terms before it reached liquidity.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation N3; calculation C4; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 88

Free cash flow is thin and rests on one lever, capital spending. Free cash flow was positive at USD 155.62 million in the nine months of 2026 against an outflow of USD 260.43 million a year earlier, but it is still an outflow of USD 23.86 million over the last twelve months, because 2025 capital spending of USD 571.81 million was cut to 6.40% of revenue from 17.26%. Operating cash flow carries little spare capacity if spending resumes.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation N4; calculation N5; calculation N6; calculation N7

Liquidity is adequate for scheduled debt service but is exposed to non-debt claims. Cash plus the undrawn revolver was USD 873.41 million, covering principal due through 2028 1.63 times, while standby letters of credit rose to USD 15.9 million from USD 1.2 million and settlements, uninsured verdicts and a USD 400.0 million past payment show how fast litigation can draw cash; house-normalised EBITDA covered interest expense 2.91x over the last twelve months.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation N2; calculation C1; calculation C3

Refinancing risk is concentrated in three years. Principal due is USD 494.73 million in 2028, USD 536.10 million in 2029 and USD 745.05 million in 2030, which is 75.04% of the total, with the revolver and term-loan balance falling due together in 2030; the notes are fixed rate and the 2025 refinancing removed any earlier bullet, but market access cannot be judged because no prices or ratings were supplied.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation N8; calculation N9; calculation N10; calculation C2

Business quality is strong on scale and diversification and weak on payor mix. The company operates facilities in 40 states and Puerto Rico, no facility is above 4% of revenue and no state above 14%, and 91% of beds outside treatment centers are in owned property excluded from the credit facility pledge, yet Medicaid supplied 61.8% of nine-month 2026 revenue, so federal and state funding decisions set the revenue base.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 10

Event risk is the main source of downside and part of it is uninsured. A federal criminal investigation and SEC subpoenas cover the acute care line, which was 57.53% of nine-month 2026 revenue, the company has settled matters at USD 400.0 million and USD 179.0 million, and a USD 35.0 million compensatory and USD 70.0 million punitive jury award against an indirect subsidiary is contested.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 20

Financial policy is neutral to supportive for creditors. No dividend has ever been paid, repurchases have stopped with USD 250.0 million of authority unused, and debt fell USD 147.61 million in 2026, but the unused authority and equity-linked pay for the chief executive leave restart as a monitoring point.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation N11
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a weak view is the direction of travel: house-normalised net leverage fell from 5.72x to 4.96x, free cash flow turned positive at USD 155.62 million in the nine months, debt fell USD 147.61 million and no behaviour in the filings extracts value from creditors. The strongest evidence for a weaker view is that the improvement comes mainly from cutting capital spending, the earnings base used for leverage is a house measure, and legal outcomes are unquantified.

The view would improve if the investigations close without a material penalty, same-facility growth holds while capital spending stays low for a further year, and the compliance certificate shows covenant room on the agreement's own definition. It would worsen if Medicaid directed-payment caps or eligibility rules reduce revenue per patient day, if an investigation or the contested jury award produces a payment near the scale of the Desert Hills settlement, or if repurchases or growth spending resume before the 2028 notes are refinanced.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C5; calculation N11
### Limitations
- Covenant earnings were not supplied, so the leverage assessment rests on a house-normalised measure and a different definition in the agreement could move it either way.
- No prices, ratings or spreads were supplied, so refinancing capacity is judged from maturity structure and liquidity alone and market access is not assessed.
- The filings contain no management forecast, so the outlook and the downside scenario are causal narratives, not projections, and cannot size a loss.
- No peer set was supplied, so the comparison with typical leveraged-credit issuers is qualitative.
### Company description

Acadia runs 280 behavioral healthcare facilities with about 12,800 beds in 40 states and Puerto Rico through the subsidiaries of a listed holding company. Acute inpatient psychiatric care was 55% of 2025 revenue, specialty treatment 17%, comprehensive treatment centers for opioid use 17% and residential treatment 11%. Demand is clinical and non-discretionary and entry is limited by licensing and certificate-of-need rules, which supports volume visibility, but 72% of revenue comes from Medicare and Medicaid at predetermined rate schedules, so cash-flow visibility rests on government budgets and the company cannot recover cost increases through price.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 42; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 43

The asset base supports refinancing confidence: 91% of beds outside treatment centers sit in owned property, maintenance capital spending is about 3% of revenue, no facility exceeds 4% of revenue and no state exceeds 14%. These features limit the damage from a single facility or state event but do not offset the payor concentration.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 11
### Ownership and group structure

No sponsor or controlling holder is identified, so there is no extraction vehicle and no equity backstop; the only investor named, Waud Capital Partners, has a charter carve-out and no stated stake. The wholly-owned U.S. subsidiaries guarantee the credit facility and the three note series, while real property is excluded from the facility pledge, and 19 facilities are held through joint ventures in which partners own 5% to 35% and hold put rights on a change of control over USD 229.88 million of redeemable interests that sit outside debt. The risk for creditors is therefore event and payor risk, not owner behaviour, and governance risk is assessed as Medium because of open investigations and leadership turnover.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation N14; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 21; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 24
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is predictable in volume but not in price. Same-facility revenue grew 4.0% in the nine months of 2026, with patient days up 1.2%, admissions up 6.5% and revenue per patient day up 2.8%, so growth is admission and price led while stays shorten. Government payors reimburse on predetermined rate schedules and Medicaid supplied 61.8% of revenue against 53.9% in 2023, which ties pricing power to state budgets and to the federal budget act that caps state directed payments from 2028. Consolidated revenue grew 5.04% in 2025 and 3.96% in the nine months of 2026, and the shift of mix toward acute inpatient care increases dependence on the line under investigation.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 38; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 43
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Margins have compressed and the cost base is largely fixed. Salaries, wages and benefits were 55.27% of nine-month 2026 revenue, the company reports a shortage of nurses and counselors that forces wage increases and costlier contract labor, and other operating expenses, mainly purchased services, insurance and provider taxes, rose to 16.7% of 2025 revenue from 14.0% and were 16.3% in the nine months of 2026 with a USD 28.6 million unfavourable liability adjustment. House-normalised EBITDA margin fell to 12.48% in 2025 from 19.82% in 2024 and was 12.94% for the last twelve months, so margins cannot be defended under volume pressure without cost action, and cost flexibility sits mainly in growth capital spending rather than operating costs.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C4; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 69; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 87; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 44
### Capital intensity and FCF conversion

EBITDA converts to free cash flow only when growth spending is cut. Maintenance capital spending is about 3% of revenue, but total spending was 17.26% of 2025 revenue and 6.40% in the nine months of 2026; operating cash flow of USD 321.48 million in the nine months funded USD 165.86 million of spending and a revolver paydown. Cash paid for interest was USD 124.66 million in 2025 against interest expense, net of USD 138.86 million, government investigation costs fell to USD 38.16 million in the nine months of 2026 from USD 123.27 million, and last-twelve-month interest cover on an accrual basis was 2.91x, so free cash flow after interest remains small.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation N12; calculation N13; calculation C3; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 29
### Porter's five forces

Rivalry is moderate and local: competitors include non-profit and government-owned providers with tax advantages and independent operators with strong reputations, which can reduce patient volume if they recruit staff or win payor contracts better. Entry is limited by licensing, accreditation and certificate-of-need approval, which protects existing beds. Substitutes matter through lower-cost settings and shorter stays, with same-facility length of stay down 5.0% in the nine months of 2026. Buyer power is high because government programs and managed care set rates, and supplier power sits mainly in scarce nurses, counselors and psychiatrists. Together these forces cap pricing and keep labor cost high, which limits margin durability.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 43; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 67; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 69; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 38
### PEST

Political and regulatory factors are a primary credit driver. The federal budget act reduces federal Medicaid spending, bars new provider taxes, caps state directed payments and requires work or community engagement rules by 2026-12-31 with six-monthly eligibility checks, and the company also faces criminal and securities investigations; economic factors matter through loss of insurance coverage after the end of enhanced marketplace subsidies. Social and technological factors do not appear to be primary credit drivers on the materials supplied, apart from cybersecurity incidents the company discloses it has experienced.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 36–37; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 63
### SWOT

Strengths are scale across 40 states, owned real estate, no facility above 4% of revenue, falling capital intensity and no extraction by owners. Weaknesses are leverage that is high on a house-normalised basis, negative reported EBITDA, thin free cash flow, a labor-heavy cost base and Medicaid dependence. Opportunities that could improve credit quality are joint venture growth funded by partners, deleveraging from lower spending and closing the investigations. Threats are Medicaid funding changes, penalties or uninsured verdicts, wage inflation and a refinancing wall in 2028 to 2030.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1)
### Financial profile and credit quality

On a ratings-style lens the financial profile is weak to average. Scale and market position are strong, competitive advantage and business diversification are average because service lines are spread but payors are concentrated, cost and capex flexibility is average because spending can be cut but labor cannot, margin stability and free cash flow stability are weak, the ability to refinance is average with market access not assessable, liquidity is average to strong, and financial policy and governance are average. The main supports are scale, owned real estate, liquidity and deleveraging since 2025; the main constraints are leverage on an unmeasured covenant basis, thin free cash flow and event risk; the trend is improving from the 2025 trough; missing datapoints are covenant earnings, market pricing and investigation outcomes.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C1; calculation C4
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

The next 12 to 24 months are decided by policy and legal dates. Medicaid work and community engagement rules must be in place by 2026-12-31, the final approval hearing for the derivative settlement is set for 2026-12-10, trial of the sixth Desert Hills lawsuit is set for 2027-04-19, and the 5.500% notes due 2028-07-01 become current in July 2027. Tailwinds are demand for behavioral care, joint venture capacity funded by partners and lower investigation costs; headwinds are Medicaid funding limits, labor cost, insurance cost and leadership transition. Over three to five years the federal cap on state directed payments steps down from 2028 and the 2028, 2029 and 2030 maturities need refinancing, so credit quality depends on holding capital spending low while rates and volumes hold.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 36–37; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23; Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1)
### Downside scenario

The initiating condition is a Medicaid rate or eligibility reduction, such as a state directed payment cap, arriving in the same period as an enforcement outcome. The first operational break is revenue per patient day, because government rate schedules do not rise with cost while salaries, wages and benefits are 55.27% of revenue, so margin falls faster than revenue. The financial transmission is lower house-normalised EBITDA against fixed debt, which lifts leverage above the 4.96x reached at 2026-09-30, while a settlement of the scale of the USD 400.0 million paid in 2024 would equal 45.80% of current liquidity of USD 873.41 million. The liquidity consequence is manageable through 2028 because liquidity covers scheduled principal 1.63 times, but the refinancing consequence is severe if leverage is high when the 2028 notes must be refinanced. Management levers are growth capital spending, held-for-sale property, the paused repurchase program and revolver availability; the observable triggers are same-facility revenue per patient day, the Medicaid share of revenue and any investigation development. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress through 2028 absent a combined shock.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C1; calculation C5; calculation N2
### Overall credit view

Overall, Acadia presents an adequate business profile supported by scale across 40 states, owned real estate and non-discretionary demand, but credit quality is constrained by leverage that is high on a house-normalised basis, negative reported EBITDA, thin free cash flow and open Medicaid and legal risks. Cash-flow durability appears weak to adequate because it depends on capital spending staying low. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on market access that is not assessable here and on leverage at the time the 2028 notes mature. The primary downside path is a Medicaid payment cut combined with a legal cash call while leverage is high. Further analysis would require the compliance certificate and covenant definitions, market prices and ratings, and investigation outcomes. Completed. Top risk: Medicaid payment reductions combined with a large uninsured legal payment.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)
### Strengths and weaknesses

Scale, diversification and owned real estate are the main strengths. The company operates 280 facilities with no facility above 4% of revenue and no state above 14%, and 91% of beds outside treatment centers are owned property excluded from the facility pledge; this spreads facility and state risk and gives lenders an unencumbered asset pool, which supports recovery relevance and refinancing confidence.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 21

Falling capital intensity and a repaid revolver are the second strength. Capital spending fell to 6.40% of revenue in the nine months of 2026 from 17.26% in 2025 and debt fell by USD 147.61 million in 2026, which turned nine-month free cash flow positive and eased house-normalised net leverage from 5.72x to 4.96x.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation N11
Creditor-neutral financial policy is the third strength. No dividend has ever been paid and repurchases stopped, so no value is extracted from creditors, although the unused authority remains.

High leverage on a house-normalised basis is the main weakness. Reported EBITDA is negative for 2025 and the last twelve months after a non-cash impairment, and house-normalised net leverage of 4.96x leaves little room for an earnings miss before refinancing.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C4

Medicaid dependence is the second weakness. Medicaid supplied 61.8% of nine-month 2026 revenue and federal changes cap state directed payments from 2028, so rate cuts would reach a labor-heavy cost base.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 36–37

Legal and regulatory event risk is the third weakness. The criminal investigation of the acute care line, a contested jury award and insurance exhaustion for some years can turn into cash calls ahead of debt reduction.
